children.text: What FHIR actually is

FHIR — Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources — is an HL7 standard for representing and moving health data. It does two things. It defines a set of discrete resources, each a structured representation of one clinical or administrative concept: Patient, Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest, Coverage, Claim. And it defines a web API convention for requesting and writing those resources, so that a client asks for a patient's lab observations the same way it would ask any modern web service for a record.

That is genuinely important. Before FHIR, connecting two systems meant negotiating a point-to-point interface: a bespoke message format, a bespoke transport, a bespoke mapping, rebuilt for every new pair of endpoints. FHIR R4, the version CMS regulation is written against, replaced most of that with a published contract.

What FHIR is not is a product. It specifies a framework that compliant systems operate within. It does not specify which optional elements a given implementation populates, what local codes get mapped to, what business rules gate a request, or what an organization will agree to share. A hospital running Epic and a critical access hospital running TruBridge can both be accurately described as FHIR R4 compliant while exchanging documents with different content, triggering different workflows, and requiring custom integration work to interoperate at all.
The four things a standard cannot do

Optionality. FHIR resources carry many optional elements. Two conformant servers can populate different subsets, and a receiving system that expected a field it does not get has a data problem the standard does not consider an error. Implementation guides — US Core, the Da Vinci guides for prior authorization and coverage — exist precisely to narrow this, and adoption of the guides is a separate question from adoption of the standard.

Semantics. FHIR moves a coded value; it does not guarantee both ends mean the same thing by it. Vocabulary alignment across ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC and RxNorm is terminology work, which is why Vermont's UHDS architecture puts terminology services in the foundational layer next to identity rather than treating them as a downstream cleanup.

Identity. FHIR assumes you know which patient you are asking about. Establishing that the record at one organization and the record at another belong to the same person is the matching problem, and the standard has nothing to say about it.

Trust and consent. Who may request what, under which authority, with what patient consent, and with what recourse when it is abused — none of that is in the specification. It lives in network agreements, state law, and 42 CFR Part 2 for substance use records.

Functional interoperability is FHIR compliance plus matching plus terminology plus event notification plus a workflow that puts the result in front of a person who can act on it. The standard supplies one of those five.
Compliant and non-interoperable at the same time

The most expensive mistake in a technology roadmap is treating FHIR compliance as a milestone rather than a precondition. A board can be shown a slide saying every hospital in the network is FHIR R4 certified and conclude the interoperability problem is closed. The operational test is different and much harder: can a care coordinator at one hospital see, today, that their patient was discharged from an emergency department at another organization last night, and act on it before the care gap opens? That requires identity resolution, an event notification subscription, a trust agreement, and a workflow. Certification gets you none of them.
The rules that made it mandatory
Two CMS rules did most of the work, and they are frequently conflated.

The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access final rule, CMS-9115-F, was published May 1, 2020. It required Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service and managed care programs, and qualified health plan issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges to stand up two FHIR APIs: a Patient Access API letting enrollees pull their claims, encounter and clinical data into a third-party app of their choosing, and a Provider Directory API. Both were required from January 1, 2021, with CMS exercising enforcement discretion until July 1, 2021.

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, CMS-0057-F, was issued January 17, 2024 and is the more operationally disruptive of the two. It applies to the same payer set and arrives in two phases. From January 1, 2026, impacted payers must decide standard prior authorization requests within 7 calendar days and expedited requests within 72 hours, must give a specific reason for every denial regardless of how the request arrived, and must publicly report prior authorization metrics. From January 1, 2027, they must operate four FHIR APIs: a Prior Authorization API, a Provider Access API, a Payer-to-Payer API, and an expanded Patient Access API that now carries prior authorization information.

Read in sequence, the two rules describe a deliberate escalation. The 2020 rule gave patients a pipe. The 2024 rule puts a payer's most contested administrative process — prior authorization — onto that pipe, with a clock attached and the metrics published.
The two CMS interoperability rules
Rule —
CMS-9115-F — Interoperability and Patient Access → CMS-0057-F — Interoperability and Prior Authorization
Issued —
May 1, 2020 → January 17, 2024
Core requirement —
Patient Access API and Provider Directory API → Prior Authorization, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer and expanded Patient Access APIs
Non-API obligations —
Admission, discharge and transfer event notifications as a Condition of Participation → 7-day standard and 72-hour expedited decisions; specific denial reasons; public metrics reporting
Key dates —
APIs required January 1, 2021; enforcement from July 1, 2021 → Process requirements January 1, 2026; APIs primarily January 1, 2027

children.text: Information blocking — the obligation that runs the other way

The CMS rules compel payers to build pipes. The 21st Century Cures Act runs in the opposite direction: it prohibits withholding data through the pipes that exist. The information blocking provisions apply to three categories of actor — health care providers, developers of certified health IT, and health information exchanges and networks — and prohibit a practice the actor knows is likely to interfere with access, exchange or use of electronic health information and knows to be unreasonable.

The regime is structured as a broad prohibition with a defined set of safe harbors. HHS has finalized nine exceptions covering situations such as preventing harm, protecting privacy, infeasibility, and the manner in which a request is fulfilled. A later addition, the TEFCA Manner Exception finalized in the HTI-2 rule, lets an actor satisfy a request via TEFCA when both parties are TEFCA participants. The exceptions are not vague principles; each carries specific conditions that must be met, and an actor either meets them or does not.

For most of the rule's life the prohibition had no teeth on the provider side. That changed. The HHS Office of Inspector General's civil monetary penalty rule took effect September 1, 2023, authorizing penalties of up to $1 million per violation against developers of certified health IT, entities offering certified health IT, and health information exchanges and networks. Then on June 24, 2024, HHS finalized the provider disincentives rule, effective July 31, 2024, which routes consequences through Medicare payment programs instead of fines.

children.text: Why the disincentives changed the calculus

Before mid-2024, a provider organization weighing whether to share data with a competitor faced an enforceable-in-theory prohibition and no defined consequence. The disincentives rule converted that into arithmetic a CFO can run. Three quarters of a hospital's annual market basket update is a material number on any operating budget, and Shared Savings Program ineligibility for at least a year is existential for an ACO. Note also who reports: the Cures Act channels complaints through a public portal, and the actors most likely to file are the competitors and vendors on the other side of the refused request.
The unsolved problem: knowing who the patient is

Every use case that crosses an organizational boundary depends on matching — establishing that the John Smith born March 14, 1952 at one hospital is the same person as the John Smith born March 14, 1952 at another, and the Jonathan Smith with that date of birth in the Medicaid enrollment file.

The United States has no national patient identifier. A congressional appropriations rider has barred HHS from spending federal funds to promulgate one since 1999, which means matching is done probabilistically on demographic attributes: name, date of birth, address, sex, sometimes phone. Those attributes are entered by humans under time pressure, stored in inconsistent formats, and change over a lifetime.

The measured consequences are worse than most executives assume. Research published by The Pew Charitable Trusts in 2018 found match rates between organizations as low as 50% — including, per work by the ONC contractor Audacious Inquiry, between organizations running the same EHR vendor, because the variability is in process and configuration rather than in the software. Measured duplicate record creation rates within organizations ranged from 0.77% to 6%. Pew also found that standardizing addresses to USPS formatting raised match rates by roughly three percentage points, which is both a real gain and a measure of how far three percentage points leaves you from solved.

A master patient index is the infrastructure that manages this. It is the least demo-able thing in a health IT portfolio — it produces no screen a board wants to look at — which is precisely why organizations buy the portal and the dashboard first and discover afterward that every care coordination feature they wanted depends on the piece they deferred.
Treat the MPI as a go/no-go gate

Before approving any multi-organization care coordination initiative, ask one question: what is our measured match rate against the organizations we intend to coordinate with, and who measured it? Not whether an MPI exists — what rate it achieves, on real records, across the boundary that matters. If nobody can answer, the initiative is being planned on an assumption, and the pattern holds in any state and any network structure, not just Vermont's.
Vermont's version of the problem

Vermont carried a self-inflicted version of the matching constraint until recently. Under 18 V.S.A. section 9410(e), state law prohibited the use of direct patient identifiers for record matching — a privacy provision that had the effect of forbidding the technique that accurate identity resolution requires. Act 167 repealed it, which is why the UHDS architecture can now place a master patient index, supplied by Verato, in its foundational layer alongside terminology services and the integration engine.

The operational picture the state is matching across is genuinely fragmented. Vermont's 14 hospitals do not share an EHR — UVM Health Network's hospitals run Epic, the independent hospitals a mix of other vendors' systems — before accounting for community mental health agencies, skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies and independent practices, many of which have no FHIR-capable system at all. Oliver Wyman's community engagement surfaced the everyday version: participants described needing to contact 31 separate EMS agencies to arrange patient transfers.

That fragmentation is the substance of the statewide EHR question Vermont has under active feasibility assessment. The analytical question is not whether one platform would be tidier. It is whether FHIR-based exchange across four existing platforms can deliver real-time bidirectional data sharing at an acceptable cost — because if it can, the case for a migration that would cost hundreds of millions and disrupt clinical workflow for years weakens considerably.
Three FHIR use cases, ranked by transformation value
Patient Access API —
Patients pull records into a third-party app of their choosing → Mandatory compliance. The gate is smaller hospitals without the IT capacity to maintain an endpoint.
Provider Access API —

A care coordinator queries clinical records held by another organization for a shared patient → Highest value for a clinically integrated network — and the use case most dependent on a working master patient index and a trust framework.
Payer-to-provider API —

Electronic prior authorization and formulary exchange via the Da Vinci CRD and DTR implementation guides → Administrative simplification. Requires both the EHR and the payer to implement complementary guides, which is why it lags the others.
TEFCA — the trust layer the standard does not supply

FHIR tells two systems how to talk. It does not tell them whether they are permitted to, or give either one recourse if the other misuses what it receives. That is the gap the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement fills: a single set of legal terms that participants sign once, rather than negotiating bilateral agreements with every counterparty.

Exchange runs through Qualified Health Information Networks designated by the Sequoia Project, which holds the Recognized Coordinating Entity contract. Eleven networks had QHIN status as of November 2025, including eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, CommonWell, Health Gorilla, KONZA and MedAllies, with Oracle Health subsequently designated. More than 23,000 organizations are live on TEFCA as QHINs, participants or subparticipants.

For a state network the practical implication is that national connectivity is now a membership decision rather than an engineering project — which matters most for exactly the encounters a state exchange cannot see. A Vermont patient treated at Dartmouth Hitchcock in New Hampshire generates a record that no Vermont-only infrastructure will ever hold.
The compliance path, in order
Sequence the work the way the dependencies run, not the way the deadlines are dated.

Identity first: measure the current match rate across the boundaries that matter and stand up or fix the master patient index. Terminology second: agree the code systems and map local vocabularies, because every downstream analysis inherits whatever is done here. Then the APIs and the implementation guides, which is where most roadmaps mistakenly begin. Then the trust and consent layer — network membership, participation agreements, and the segregated handling that 42 CFR Part 2 requires for substance use records. Then, last, the workflow integration that puts an exchanged record in front of someone at the moment they are making a decision.

An organization that reverses this order arrives at a defensible compliance posture and an unusable system. It will hold certifications, satisfy auditors, and still not be able to tell a care coordinator that their patient was in another hospital's emergency department last night.

summary: FHIR is a standard, not a product, and two systems can both be certified and still fail to exchange anything useful. This lesson covers what the standard actually specifies, the CMS rules and information blocking penalties that made it mandatory, and the patient matching problem none of it solves.
